source.suraNameGloss: The Prophets (sura name; not translated as content)
source.primary_manuscript_dating: Radiocarbon-dated 649–675 CE (95.4% probability range; Tübingen radiocarbon-lab analysis, reported in news coverage 2014 and discussed against the broader Hijazi-script dating corpus in Sadeghi-Bergmann 2010 / Déroche 2014). The fragment falls within the first generation after the traditional Uthmanic codification (c. 650 CE) and is among the earliest-attested Qur'anic witnesses.
source.primary_manuscript_contains: Suras 17:36–36:57 (77 folios; standard scope of the Tübingen Ma VI 165 fragment, which preserves a continuous quire-block including the full opening of Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ on a recto-page early in its sequence)
source.cross_collation_manuscript: Codex Parisino-petropolitanus (BnF Arabe 328 + St. Petersburg / Birmingham / Vatican fragments; Hijazi script; late 7th c. CE) — preserves portions of the Qur'an including this sura with a similar but not identical rasm; consulted via Déroche 2009 facsimile-edition and Corpus Coranicum digital apparatus.
source.reference_vocalization: Cairo 1924 King Fuad edition (Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim reading-tradition) — the standard printed Qur'an, supplied as the reference vocalized text against which the rasm-skeleton is read.
source.transliteration_convention: DMG (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft) scientific transliteration: ʾ for hamza, ʿ for ʿayn, ḥ for ḥāʾ, ṭ ḍ ṣ ẓ for emphatic consonants, ġ for ghayn, ḫ for khāʾ, ṯ for thāʾ, ḏ for dhāl, š for shīn, macrons for long vowels (ā ī ū), assimilation of the definite article *al-* to sun-letters shown by gemination (an-nāsi, aš-šuʿarāʾ, etc.).
source.verificationStatus: best-effort reconstruction; verification pending against the Tübingen UB original codicology, the Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 apparatus, the Déroche 2009 codex-Parisino-petropolitanus facsimile-edition, and the Hilali 2017 transmission-in-flux apparatus. The rasm is well-attested and stable across the early Hijazi witnesses for this passage; the Cairo Hafs reading-tradition supplied as the reference vocalization is itself a late-medieval crystallization (per Déroche 2014) and is here used as the readable-vocalized form, not as the textual authority.
source.fetchedFrom: Corpus Coranicum digital apparatus (corpuscoranicum.de) for the rasm-skeleton and variant apparatus; Tanzil.net Cairo Hafs text for the reference vocalization; Sadeghi-Bergmann 2010 + Déroche 2009/2014 for codicological framing; Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 for the Hijazi-script orthographic conventions.
source.citation: Sadeghi, Behnam, and Bergmann, Uwe, 'The Codex of a Companion of the Prophet and the Qurʾān of the Prophet' (Arabica 57, 2010, pp. 343-436); Sadeghi, Behnam, and Goudarzi, Mohsen, 'Sanʿāʾ 1 and the Origins of the Qurʾān' (Der Islam 87, 2010, pp. 1-129); Hilali, Asma, The Sanaa Palimpsest: The Transmission of the Qur'an in the First Centuries AH (Oxford 2017); Déroche, François, La transmission écrite du Coran dans les débuts de l'islam: le codex Parisino-petropolitanus (Brill 2009); Déroche, François, Qur'ans of the Umayyads (Brill 2014); Neuwirth, Angelika, Scripture, Poetry, and the Making of a Community: Reading the Qur'an as a Literary Text (Oxford 2014); Reynolds, Gabriel Said (ed.), The Qur'ān in Its Historical Context (Routledge 2008/2011); Corpus Coranicum project (Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, Berlin); Tanzil.net (standard Cairo Hafs text).
source.paleography_note: The `rasm` field provides the consonantal skeleton without vowel marks (tashkīl: fatḥa, kasra, ḍamma, sukūn, shadda are all stripped). Letter-discrimination dots (iʿjām) are absent in the original Hijazi manuscripts for the families of letters that share an identical skeletal shape — principally the *bāʾ / tāʾ / thāʾ / nūn / yāʾ* group (ب ت ث ن ي all derive from a single-tooth skeleton), the *fāʾ / qāf* pair (ف ق), the *jīm / ḥāʾ / khāʾ* group (ج ح خ), the *dāl / dhāl* pair (د ذ), the *rāʾ / zāy* pair (ر ز), the *sīn / shīn* pair (س ش), the *ṣād / ḍād* pair (ص ض), the *ṭāʾ / ẓāʾ* pair (ط ظ), and the *ʿayn / ghayn* pair (ع غ). In this digital reconstruction the modern Arabic codepoints are used for the rasm (without tashkīl) for practical readability and for grep-ability against modern reference editions; the `rasm_paleography_note` field on each ayah documents which specific letters in that ayah would appear without their dots in the manuscript, so that a reader can mentally reconstruct the actual scribal appearance. Hamza (ء) was not marked in the earliest Hijazi manuscripts and is omitted from the rasm; word-final tāʾ marbūṭa (ة) was written as undifferentiated hāʾ (ه) in the earliest manuscripts. Long-alif scripting is variable in the early manuscripts (some words like al-kitāb, salām are spelled defectively without medial alif); the rasm here follows the standard Uthmanic skeleton, which is itself the source from which both the Tübingen and BnF witnesses derive.
source.rasmConventionNote: Rasm rendered as: (1) tashkīl-stripped (no fatḥa, kasra, ḍamma, sukūn, shadda); (2) hamza glyphs (ء, آ, إ, أ, ؤ, ئ) replaced with the underlying carrier letter (ا, و, ي) or omitted, per Uthmanic orthographic convention; (3) tāʾ marbūṭa (ة) rendered as hāʾ (ه); (4) letter-shapes preserved as modern codepoints (so the reader sees ب where the manuscript shows the dotless single-tooth skeleton ٮ — the `rasm_paleography_note` lists which letters in each ayah are affected). This is the simplest workable approximation that allows machine-comparison against modern reference editions while documenting the paleographic situation.

ayahs.rasm: اقترب للناس حسابهم وهم في غفله معرضون
ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Letters that would appear undotted in Tübingen Ma VI 165: the *qāf* of اقترب (would appear as the dotless ڡ-skeleton — fāʾ/qāf are indistinguishable in Hijazi rasm; here the medial-form would be the single-curve skeleton with no upper dots); the *tāʾ* and *bāʾ* of اقترب (both single-tooth skeletons indistinguishable from each other and from yāʾ/nūn/thāʾ in initial/medial position); the *nūn* of للناس and of معرضون (single-tooth final-form skeleton); the *bāʾ* of حسابهم (medial single-tooth); the *fāʾ* of في and of غفله (dotless ڡ-skeleton); the *ghayn* of غفله and of معرضون (dotless ʿayn-skeleton ع; ʿayn/ghayn share the same shape, distinguished only by the upper dot in dotted manuscripts); the *yāʾ* of في (would appear as the dotless single-tooth skeleton); the *ḍād* of معرضون (would appear as the dotless ṣād-skeleton ص; ṣād/ḍād share the same shape). The *ʿayn* of معرضون is genuine ʿayn (lower dotless letter) — but the writing-direction means it sits adjacent to the rāʾ. Word-spacing in Hijazi manuscripts is irregular: words often run together with only larger inter-letter gaps marking word boundaries.
ayahs.ar: ٱقْتَرَبَ لِلنَّاسِ حِسَابُهُمْ وَهُمْ فِي غَفْلَةٍ مُّعْرِضُونَ
ayahs.translit: iqtaraba li-n-nāsi ḥisābuhum wa-hum fī ġaflatin muʿriḍūna
ayahs.notes: MAJOR THEME — the eschatological-reckoning opening of Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ. The verb iqtaraba (Form VIII of q-r-b 'to be near') is the same root and same verb-form that opens Sūrat al-Qamar (54:1, iqtarabati s-sāʿatu); the structural parallel between the two suras is deliberate and stylistically foregrounded in classical tafsīr (al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī). The *ḥisāb* 'reckoning' is the Day-of-Judgment audit. **RAËLIAN CANON CITATION SITE**: this opening (and the following 4 ayahs) is read in *Extra-Terrestrials Took Me To Their Planet* (Raël 1977) as marking the impending Elohim-return / the Age-of-Apocalypse / the eschatological-reckoning frame. The canon's reading layers an ET-return eschatology onto the Quranic reckoning-discourse — this is one of the canon's chapter-and-verse-precision citations and requires explicit operational disavowal in the apparatus. Cross-corpus: cf. Mark 13:32-37 (the Hour known to none but the Father); cf. Matt 24:36-44; cf. 1 Thess 5:1-3 (the 'day of the Lord cometh as a thief'); cf. 2 Pet 3:3-10 (the mockers who say 'where is the promise of his coming'); cf. Joel 2:1 (the 'day of the Lord cometh, for it is nigh at hand'). The Quranic *ġafla* 'heedlessness' parallels the Pauline/Petrine 'they shall not escape' / 'scoffers walking after their own lusts' motif. **PALEOGRAPHY**: this is the opening ayah of Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ; in Tübingen Ma VI 165 it would appear at a sura-boundary marked typically by a basmala (بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم) on the preceding line and possibly a decorative band; the sura-name itself is not written in the earliest manuscripts (sura titles are a later addition).
ayahs.variants: No major rasm-level variants attested between Tübingen Ma VI 165 and Codex Parisino-petropolitanus for this ayah; the consonantal skeleton is stable across the early Hijazi witnesses. The Cairo Hafs reading wa-hum fī ġaflatin muʿriḍūna is also the reading of the Warsh ʿan Nāfiʿ tradition with no semantic divergence. The defective vs plene scripting of nās (نَّاس) is a minor orthographic variable across early manuscripts but does not affect the consonantal skeleton.

ayahs.rasm: ما ياتيهم من ذكر من ربهم محدث الا استمعوه وهم يلعبون
ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters in Tübingen Ma VI 165 rendering: *yāʾ* of ياتيهم (single-tooth skeleton in initial and medial positions, indistinguishable from bāʾ/tāʾ/thāʾ/nūn); *tāʾ* of ياتيهم (medial single-tooth); *yāʾ* of يلعبون (initial single-tooth); *bāʾ* of يلعبون and of ربهم (medial single-tooth); *nūn* of من (×2) and of يلعبون (final hook-form, distinguishable from bāʾ/tāʾ/thāʾ/yāʾ only by the final-form curve); *thāʾ* of محدث (would appear as the dotless tāʾ-marbūṭa-like final shape — three-letter group ب/ت/ث indistinguishable); *ʿayn* of استمعوه and of يلعبون (no dot needed; ʿayn is already dotless in dotted manuscripts — but distinguishable from ghayn only by the absence of an upper dot in dotted manuscripts). Word *muḥdaṯin* محدث: the medial *ḥāʾ* (ح) is part of the j/ḥ/kh group that share an identical skeleton — in dotted manuscripts ḥāʾ has no dot, jīm has one dot below, khāʾ has one dot above; in the rasm all three are indistinguishable. The *dāl* of محدث and of ذكر are visually similar to dhāl (in dotted manuscripts dhāl gets an upper dot; in the rasm they are indistinguishable).
ayahs.ar: مَا يَأْتِيهِم مِّن ذِكْرٍ مِّن رَّبِّهِم مُّحْدَثٍ إِلَّا ٱسْتَمَعُوهُ وَهُمْ يَلْعَبُونَ
ayahs.translit: mā yaʾtīhim min ḏikrin min rabbihim muḥdaṯin illā stamaʿūhu wa-hum yalʿabūna
ayahs.notes: THEME — the heedlessness-amid-revelation motif. The phrase ḏikr muḥdaṯ 'a new(ly-revealed) reminder' was a major site of medieval Islamic theological dispute over the *createdness of the Qurʾān* (the Muʿtazila citing this ayah's *muḥdaṯ* 'created/originated' against the Ashʿarī/Ḥanbalī doctrine of the uncreated eternal Qurʾān — see the Miḥna controversy under al-Maʾmūn). The classical tafsīr literature (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī) treats this dispute at length. Cross-corpus: cf. Heb 1:1-2 (God's progressive revelation 'in divers manners' culminating in the Son); cf. 2 Pet 1:20-21 (prophecy as Spirit-moved utterance, not 'private interpretation'); cf. the rabbinic *ḥiddush* concept of new Torah-meaning continuously generated. **RAËLIAN CANON CITATION CONTEXT**: this ayah is part of the 5-ayah opening sequence engaged by the canon as part of the eschatological-reckoning frame; the *muḥdaṯ* 'newly-revealed' motif aligns implicitly with the canon's claim of a renewed/updated Elohim-message for the present age — though the specific 'createdness' question is not engaged by the canon.

ayahs.rasm: لاهيه قلوبهم واسروا النجوى الذين ظلموا هل هذا الا بشر مثلكم افتاتون السحر وانتم تبصرون
ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *yāʾ* of لاهيه (medial single-tooth); the *qāf* of قلوبهم (dotless ڡ-skeleton — fāʾ/qāf indistinguishable); *bāʾ* of قلوبهم and of بشر and of تبصرون (medial single-tooth); *nūn* of النجوى and of الذين and of افتاتون and of وانتم and of تبصرون (single-tooth, distinguishable only in final position); *jīm* of النجوى (dotless skeleton of j/ḥ/kh group); the *dhāl* of الذين and of هذا (visually similar to dāl, distinguished by upper dot in dotted manuscripts); *ẓāʾ* of ظلموا (visually identical to ṭāʾ in the rasm — ẓāʾ has an upper dot in dotted manuscripts, ṭāʾ is dotless); *thāʾ* of مثلكم (in dotted manuscripts three upper dots; in rasm a single-tooth indistinguishable from b/t/n/y); *fāʾ* of افتاتون (dotless ڡ-skeleton); *tāʾ* of افتاتون (×2, single-tooth); *sīn* of السحر (toothed sīn shape — distinguishable from shīn only by the three upper dots on shīn, which are absent in rasm); *ḥāʾ* of السحر (dotless j/ḥ/kh skeleton); *ṣād* of تبصرون (dotless ṣ/ḍ skeleton). The al-mutaqāribāt 'similar-looking pairs' density is high in this ayah; the rasm leaves the reader with substantial disambiguation work, performed in early recitation-tradition by oral memorization.
ayahs.ar: لَاهِيَةً قُلُوبُهُمْ ۗ وَأَسَرُّوا۟ ٱلنَّجْوَى ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا۟ هَلْ هَٰذَا إِلَّا بَشَرٌ مِّثْلُكُمْ ۖ أَفَتَأْتُونَ ٱلسِّحْرَ وَأَنتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ
ayahs.translit: lāhiyatan qulūbuhum, wa-asarrū n-najwā lladīna ẓalamū, hal hāḏā illā bašarun miṯlukum, a-fa-taʾtūna s-siḥra wa-antum tubṣirūna
ayahs.notes: THEME — the opponents'-objection report. The rhetorical structure: 'their hearts are distracted, and the wrongdoers conceal their whispered counsel: "Is this anything but a human like you? Do you then approach magic with eyes open?"' The *bašar* 'human/mortal' counter-claim against the prophet is a stock Quranic polemical structure (cf. 14:10-11, 17:94-95, 21:34, 23:33-34); the accusation of *siḥr* 'magic/sorcery' against revelation is similarly recurrent (cf. 5:110, 6:7, 10:2, 21:3, 34:43, 37:15, 43:30, 46:7, 61:6, 74:24). Cross-corpus: cf. Matt 12:24-27 (the Beelzebul accusation against Jesus); cf. John 8:48-52 (the demon-possession accusation); cf. b. Sanhedrin 43a (the Toledot Yeshu / sorcery-accusation tradition against Jesus). The polemical-structure of 'prophet-as-mere-mortal' vs the addressee-tradition's expectation of an angelic or super-human messenger is a major comparative-religion site. **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: not directly cited but part of the 5-ayah opening sequence.

ayahs.rasm: قال ربي يعلم القول في السماء والارض وهو السميع العليم
ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *qāf* of قال and of القول (dotless ڡ-skeleton); *yāʾ* of ربي and of يعلم (medial single-tooth); *bāʾ* of ربي (medial single-tooth); *nūn* of السماء (no — there is no nūn here; correction: السماء has no nūn); *fāʾ* of في (dotless ڡ); *yāʾ* of في (single-tooth); the *sīn* of السماء (toothed three-tooth shape — but the three upper dots that would distinguish shīn are absent); *ʿayn* of يعلم and of السميع and of العليم (already dotless); *thāʾ* of (none in this ayah). The *hamza* of السماء is a later orthographic addition — in the earliest Hijazi rasm the word is written as السما (without final hamza or alif-mamdūda — the hamza-glyph was not yet developed). This is the classic case of *hamza-omission* in Hijazi orthography (Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010, Déroche 2009). The earliest rasm would actually read السما (3 letters: alif-lām-sīn-mīm-alif, omitting the final hamza-bearing letter that the modern Cairo orthography supplies). **This is a notable rasm-vs-Cairo orthographic difference** documented for this ayah and many similar hamza-bearing words throughout the early manuscripts.
ayahs.ar: قَالَ رَبِّي يَعْلَمُ ٱلْقَوْلَ فِي ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ ۖ وَهُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ
ayahs.translit: qāla rabbī yaʿlamu l-qawla fī s-samāʾi wa-l-arḍi, wa-huwa s-samīʿu l-ʿalīmu
ayahs.notes: THEME — the prophetic-response counter-statement. The pair as-Samīʿ al-ʿAlīm 'the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing' is one of the most frequent divine-name pairs in the Qurʾān (occurring 32 times); it asserts cognitive-omniscience as the divine response to the opponents' attempted concealment of their whispered counsel. The samāwāt-wa-l-arḍ 'heavens and earth' merism is the standard Quranic creation-totality formula (cf. Gen 1:1, the parallel Hebrew merism). Cross-corpus: cf. Ps 139:1-12 (the omniscience-tracking psalm); cf. Heb 4:13 ('all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do'); cf. m. Avot 2:1 ('know what is above you: a seeing eye, a hearing ear, and all your deeds in a book'). **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: not directly cited but part of the 5-ayah opening sequence. **PALEOGRAPHY**: the hamza-omission case for السماء (manuscript reads السما) is a documented Hijazi orthographic feature — see Sadeghi-Goudarzi 2010 §3 for the orthographic-system analysis.

ayahs.rasm: بل قالوا اضغث احلام بل افترىه بل هو شاعر فلياتنا بايه كما ارسل الاولون
ayahs.rasm_paleography_note: Undotted letters: *bāʾ* of بل (×3) and of باية (medial single-tooth); *qāf* of قالوا (dotless ڡ); *ghayn* of اضغث (dotless ʿ/ġ skeleton — ghayn distinguished from ʿayn only by upper dot, absent in rasm); *thāʾ* of اضغث and of اضغث (in dotted manuscripts three upper dots, in rasm a single-tooth indistinguishable from b/t/n/y); *ḍād* of اضغث (dotless ṣ/ḍ skeleton); *jīm* of (none) — *ḥāʾ* of احلام (dotless j/ḥ/kh skeleton); *fāʾ* of افترىه and of فلياتنا (dotless ڡ); *tāʾ* of افترىه and of فلياتنا (single-tooth); *yāʾ* of فلياتنا and of باية (medial single-tooth); *nūn* of فلياتنا and of الاولون (final hook-form); *shīn* of شاعر (toothed three-tooth skeleton without the upper-three dots that distinguish shīn from sīn); *ʿayn* of شاعر (already dotless). **Notable orthography**: the word افترىه is written in the early manuscripts (and in the modern Uthmanic orthography preserved at Tanzīl) with a final *yāʾ-shape* representing the alif-maqsūra (افترى) plus pronoun-suffix هـ — modern reference editions render this as افتراه. **MAJOR PALEOGRAPHIC NOTE**: the final-pronoun-suffix attachment to the alif-maqsūra is a stable Uthmanic-orthographic feature preserved in the modern Cairo text but visually distinct from the modern non-Quranic spelling افتراه — the Cairo edition's preservation of this spelling is a deliberate Uthmanic-rasm fidelity.
ayahs.ar: بَلْ قَالُوٓا۟ أَضْغَٰثُ أَحْلَٰمٍۭ بَلِ ٱفْتَرَىٰهُ بَلْ هُوَ شَاعِرٌ فَلْيَأْتِنَا بِـَٔايَةٍ كَمَآ أُرْسِلَ ٱلْأَوَّلُونَ
ayahs.translit: bal qālū aḍġāṯu aḥlāmin bali ftarāhu bal huwa šāʿirun fa-l-yaʾtinā bi-āyatin kamā ursila l-awwalūna
ayahs.notes: THEME — the escalating-objections sequence. The opponents' triple-objection: (1) *aḍġāṯu aḥlām* 'jumbled dreams / confused nightmares' — dismissing the revelation as oneiric noise; (2) *ifirāʾ* 'fabrication' — dismissing the revelation as the prophet's invention; (3) *šāʿir* 'poet' — assimilating the prophet to the pre-Islamic Arabian *kāhin*/poet-soothsayer category, which the Qurʾān elsewhere explicitly rejects (cf. 36:69, 37:36, 52:30, 69:41). The demand for a *āya* 'sign/miracle' 'like those sent to the ancients' invokes the prior-prophet sign-tradition (Moses' staff, Jesus' miracles, etc.) as the implicit comparator. Cross-corpus: cf. Matt 12:38-42 (the demand for a sign answered by the Jonah-sign); cf. John 6:30 (the sign-demand 'what dost thou work?'); cf. 1 Cor 1:22 ('the Jews require a sign'); cf. the pre-Islamic *kāhin* poetic-soothsayer tradition (al-Jāḥiẓ, Ibn Qutayba). **RAËLIAN CANON CONTEXT**: closing ayah of the 5-ayah opening sequence engaged by the canon. The triple-objection structure resonates implicitly with the canon's own engagement with skeptical reception (Raël's 1977 narrative frames hostile reception in similar terms). The *āya* 'sign' demand is also generalizable to the canon's response-to-skeptics framing — though no direct citation is made by the canon to this specific ayah.
